points.title: whereas/while (for showing contrast and differences)
examples: Breakfast shops in Taiwan often serve items like soy milk and scallion pancakes, whereas in Japan, breakfast is commonly centered around rice, miso soup, and grilled fish.
People in Taiwan might talk quietly on the metro, whereas in Japan, it is considered polite to remain completely silent.
In Taiwan, it is normal to share dishes with others at the same table, whereas in Japan, everyone typically has their own set portion and uses individual chopsticks for serving shared dishes.
Taiwanese people usually greet with a casual "hello" or a handshake, whereas Japanese people bow as a traditional form of greeting.

items.sentence: When people draw or spray-paint pictures or words onto a wall, under bridges, or even on the sides of buses and trains, these pictures or words *are called* graffiti.
items.pattern: Adverbial clause (When...) + S + Passive verb phrase + C

items.sentence: It *comes in* all shapes and sizes, from simple words to detailed paintings.
items.pattern: S + Vi (Phrasal verb) + O + Prepositional phrase

items.sentence: Some *love* it, while others hate it.
The question *is*: *Is* graffiti a form of art or just a mess?
items.pattern: S + Vl + C + Direct interrogative clause

items.sentence: Graffiti *is* obviously art.
First, it *takes* a lot of time and hard work.
It *is* not just scribbling.
Graffiti artists *are* like other painters.
Their art *starts* as sketches and outlines, perfected with vivid pictures and various details later.
The only difference *is* that they paint on walls rather than on paper.
Second, like other art forms, graffiti *is* about expressing one's feelings and being creative.
items.pattern: Adverbial phrase + S + Vl + C + Gerund phrases

items.sentence: Banksy, for example, *is* a famous graffiti artist who paints to show his opinions.
items.pattern: S + Parenthetical phrase + Vl + C + Relative clause (who...)

items.sentence: Many of his works *contrast* the horror of war with the innocence of children.
In one of his pieces, a young boy *places* a flower into a soldier's gun.
items.pattern: Prepositional phrase + S + Vt + O + Prepositional phrase

items.sentence: The gun *represents* violence, whereas the flower stands for peace.
Works like this *call attention to* the need for positive change in the world.
items.pattern: S + Vt (Phrasal verb) + O + Prepositional phrase

items.sentence: *Isn't* it art?
Graffiti *makes* a mess.
It *is* nothing but visual pollution.
Most graffiti *is* "tagging," which is more like just scribbling someone's name.
These ugly paintings *make* cities look messy.
In addition, most graffiti *is done* without permission.
items.pattern: Adverbial phrase + S + Passive verb phrase + Prepositional phrase

items.sentence: A lot of money and effort *are needed* to get rid of it.
items.pattern: Compound S + Passive verb phrase + Infinitival phrase

items.sentence: The city of Los Angeles, for example, *has* a huge problem with graffiti, spending millions of dollars every year cleaning it up.
items.pattern: S + Parenthetical phrase + Vt + O + Participial phrase

items.sentence: Each month, workers *wash away* hundreds of thousands of square feet of it.
items.pattern: Adverbial phrase + S + Vt (Phrasal verb) + O

items.sentence: Even worse, graffiti *harms* communities.
Many people *believe* that graffiti is associated with criminal activity, feeling that it is unsafe to walk around or live in areas with graffiti.
items.pattern: S + Vt + Noun clause (that...) + Participial phrase with Noun clause

items.sentence: If graffiti causes all these problems, can we really *call* it art?
items.pattern: Adverbial clause (If...) + Interrogative: S + Vt + O + C

items.sentence: Which side of the wall *are* you on when it comes to graffiti?
items.pattern: Interrogative: C + Vl + S + Adverbial clause (when...)

items.sentence: *Is* it creative or destructive?
Now, it *is* your turn to express yourself and share your thoughts about it!
items.pattern: Adverb + S + Vl + C + Infinitival phrases

text_genre.raw_text: The text, "Fighting For or Against Graffiti," as its name suggests, is an argumentative essay discussing the pros and cons of graffiti. Two views are listed separately: graffiti is obviously art, and graffiti makes a mess. Each argument is presented following the structure of OREO: Opinion, Reason(s), Example(s), and Opinion (restatement). Which argument convinced you more, and why?
